# generics

```go
import "carswell.tech/x/generics"
```

Package generics provides small, general\-purpose generic helpers that fill gaps in what Go's type system otherwise makes awkward to express inline:

- [Zero](<#Zero>): the zero value of a type parameter, as a value rather than via a "var zero T" declaration.
- [MinMax](<#MinMax>): the minimum and maximum representable values of an integer or float type.
- [Signed](<#Signed>): whether an integer type is signed.
- [Ptr](<#Ptr>): the address of a value, including literals and other non\-addressable expressions.
- [Default](<#Default>) and [Deref](<#Deref>): safely read through a possibly\-nil pointer, substituting a fallback value or the zero value respectively.

<a name="Default"></a>
## func [Default](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/deref.go#L4>)

```go
func Default[T any](p *T, def T) T
```

Default returns \*p, or def if p is nil.

<a name="Deref"></a>
## func [Deref](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/deref.go#L13>)

```go
func Deref[T any](p *T) T
```

Deref returns \*p, or the zero value of T if p is nil. It is equivalent to Default\(p, Zero\[T\]\(\)\).

<a name="MinMax"></a>
## func [MinMax](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/minmax.go#L21>)

```go
func MinMax[T constraints.Integer | constraints.Float]() (min T, max T)
```

MinMax returns the minimum and maximum representable values of T, for every integer and float type in the standard library: int8 through int64 and uint8 through uint64 \(plus int, uint, and uintptr\), and float32 / float64. For float32 and float64, the bounds returned are the most negative and most positive finite values \(\-math.MaxFloat32/64 and \+math.MaxFloat32/64\), not negative/positive infinity.

MinMax determines T's bounds via a type switch on T's exact dynamic type, so it only recognizes the types listed above — a named type with one of those underlying types \(e.g. "type Meters int64"\) is not matched and causes MinMax to panic with "unsupported type", even though such a type satisfies the constraints.Integer | constraints.Float constraint.

<a name="Ptr"></a>
## func [Ptr](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/ptr.go#L7>)

```go
func Ptr[T any](v T) *T
```

Ptr returns a pointer to a new variable holding v. It is useful for taking the address of a value that isn't itself addressable, such as a literal or the result of an expression \(e.g. Ptr\(5\) or Ptr\(x\+1\), neither of which can be written as &5 or &\(x\+1\)\).

<a name="Signed"></a>
## func [Signed](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/signed.go#L9>)

```go
func Signed[I constraints.Integer]() bool
```

Signed reports whether I is a signed integer type. It works by comparing the bitwise complement of zero \(all bits set\) against zero: for a signed type this is \-1, which is less than zero; for an unsigned type it's the type's maximum value, which is not.

<a name="Zero"></a>
## func [Zero](<https://github.com/dccarswell/go/blob/main/x/generics/zero.go#L8>)

```go
func Zero[T any]() T
```

Zero returns the zero value of T. It is useful in generic code where a zero value is needed as an expression \(e.g. a function argument or return value\) rather than via a "var zero T" declaration.
